html:
The Battle of Tippecanoe was fought on 7 November 1811 near Prophetstown, where the Tippecanoe River meets the Wabash, in today's Indiana. A United States force under William Henry Harrison beat off an attack by warriors of Tecumseh's confederacy and burned their town.

The Shawnee leader Tecumseh and his brother Tenskwatawa, called the Prophet, were building an alliance of many nations to stop the sale of Native land. Prophetstown was its centre. Harrison, governor of Indiana Territory, had bought about three million acres by treaty in 1809, which Tecumseh refused to accept. In 1811, while Tecumseh was away seeking allies, Harrison marched on the town with about 1,000 men. Before dawn several hundred warriors attacked his camp. After two hours they ran low on ammunition and withdrew. Harrison lost about 190 men killed and wounded. The next day he burned the empty town and its winter food.

The Prophet lost much of his standing. Tecumseh rebuilt the alliance and joined the British in the War of 1812, which many Americans blamed partly on British support for the tribes. He was killed at the Battle of the Thames. Harrison won the presidency in 1840 as the hero of "Tippecanoe".
